ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, SC 2000, c 17, as amended; Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Regulations, SOR/2002-189; Registration Regulations, SOR/2007-121; Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46, s 462.31 (laundering proceeds of crime) and Part II.1 (terrorist financing); Special Economic Measures Act, SC 1992, c 17; United Nations Act, SC 1995, c 5; Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Sergei Magnitsky Act), SC 2017, c 20; Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9 (ABCA), ss 22 and 101-113; Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, ss 21.1-21.4 (federal ULC alternative and individual with significant control register); Alberta Corporate Registry Regulations and official registry policy directives.

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory negative screening of every director, officer, authorized signatory and ultimate beneficial owner against the consolidated Canadian sanctions list (Global Affairs Canada), the United Nations Security Council consolidated list, the Criminal Code listed-entities and listed-persons regulations, the US OFAC SDN and consolidated non-SDN lists, and, where relevant to the international licensing footprint, the UK and EU consolidated sanctions lists. Mandatory political-exposure-person (PEP) screening of domestic and foreign PEPs and heads of international organizations for a rolling 24-month lookback preceding incorporation, with enhanced due diligence where any PEP, HIO, or persons connected to sanctioned jurisdictions are identified. All screening results must be documented in the AML fit-and-proper file under FINTRAC record-keeping expectations and re-screened annually.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry / Alberta Corporate Registry System (ACRS), operated by Service Alberta, accessible via https://www.alberta.ca/corporate-registry
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta) and Alberta Corporate Registry policy, a corporate name must contain a distinctive element, a descriptive element, and the prescribed legal element; for an Alberta unlimited liability corporation the legal element must be 'ULC' or, in full form, 'Unlimited Liability Corporation'. Names must be registered in Latin-alphabet characters (English and/or French). Where the underlying commercial name is in a non-Latin script (Chinese, Cyrillic, Arabic or similar), the statutory name must be a romanized transliteration; the registry records the transliterated form on the certificate of incorporation and in ACRS, and the native-script version may appear only as a translation of the name in marketing and licensing materials. French diacritical marks are permitted. Special characters, punctuation creating ambiguity, or a name suggesting a different legal form or connection to a natural person without consent are restricted.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9 — Part 2 (Incorporation, ss. 8-13), Part 14.1 (Unlimited Liability Corporations, ss. 214.1 et seq.), s. 106 (directors), s. 25 (share consideration); Corporate Registry Regulation, Alta Reg 114/2007 (fees and forms).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Corporate Registry Division, Service Alberta (online filing via the RegistryX/CORES platform operated by Terra Nova Connections as the Province's authorized registry service provider); filings may also be submitted through licensed Alberta Registry Agents.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation (Form 1) with mandatory unlimited-liability clause, together with Notice of Registered Office (Form 4), Notice of Directors (Form 3), and Consent to Act as Director (Form 2)
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: None. The ABCA imposes no minimum paid-up capital, no escrow, and no capital deposit for Alberta ULCs; shares may be issued for cash, property, or past services at a consideration fixed by the directors (s. 25). The ULC's distinguishing feature is that shareholders remain jointly and severally liable for the corporation's debts, which is a statutory liability substitution, not a capital funding requirement. US owners may file IRS Form 8832 (check-the-box) to treat the ULC as a disregarded/partnership entity.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED that the Board approves the subscription, allotment and issuance of the Corporation's common shares in the amounts recorded in the Share Subscription Ledger, with consideration fixed by the directors per section 25 of the Business Corporations Act (Alberta); no minimum paid-up capital or escrow is required. RESOLVED FURTHER that the registered office is fixed at [registered office address], Calgary, Alberta, Canada, and the Notice of Registered Office is authorized for filing. RESOLVED FURTHER that [Name] is appointed Chief Executive Officer, [Name] Chief Financial Officer, and [Name] Corporate Secretary, to serve until successors are elected. RESOLVED FURTHER that officers are authorized to open bank accounts, execute contracts, engage counsel, and file any U.S. check-the-box election and registrations.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada (ARC) — https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html; GST/HST online portal: https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/digital-services-individuals/gst-hst-netfile.html
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A non-resident entity carrying on business in Canada must obtain a federal Business Number (BN) via the CRA's Business Registration Online (BRO) system. For GST/HST purposes, the ULC must register for a GST/HST account using the BN 'RT' program account. Registration can be completed online through BRO, by mail using Form RC1 (Request for a Business Number and Certain Program Accounts), or by telephone. The ULC must provide its legal name, Alberta corporate access number, registered office address, and description of commercial activity (NAICS 512240). If the entity is a non-resident without permanent establishment in Canada, it must still register for GST/HST if it makes taxable supplies in Canada or solicits orders in Canada, subject to the 'non-resident registrant' rules. A simplified non-resident GST/HST registration is available under Form RC1 and may require a Canadian resident representative for service of process if the non-resident has no place of business in Canada. The CRA normally issues the BN immediately in the case of online registration and by mail within 5-10 business days for paper applications. The entity must also register with the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration for provincial corporate income tax administration (Alberta levies a flat provincial corporate tax administered by the CRA under a federal-provincial tax collection agreement, so a separate Alberta corporate tax registration is not required; however, if the ULC carries on a commercial activity or has a physical presence in Alberta, it should complete the Alberta Corporate Tax Registration via the CRA's BRO system). For payroll, the ULC would need a CRA payroll deductions program account (RP) if it has Canadian employees; for import/export, an importer/exporter account (RM) must be added to the BN. The customs account is obtained through the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) via the CRA Business Registration Online interface or the CBSA Portal (Account Registration and Security Management portal). If the ULC is resident in Alberta for corporate tax purposes, it must file an annual T2 Corporation Income Tax Return; if classified as a partnership or disregarded entity for Canadian tax purposes, the ULC may be treated as a corporation under the Income Tax Act (Canada) unless it validly elects otherwise under section 216 or relies on an applicable tax treaty; in all cases a T2 return is required for corporations, while a Canadian-resident ULC that is fiscally transparent under a treaty may need to file a T2 as a deemed resident corporation. The ULC should procure a BN (9-digit) and confirm the applicable CRA program accounts: RT (GST/HST), RC (corporate income tax), RP (payroll), and RM (customs).

stage_3.statutory_election_mechanisms: Under the Income Tax Act (Canada), a ULC is generally a corporation and is taxed at the entity level as a Canadian resident corporation if it is incorporated in Alberta. However, for U.S. federal tax purposes, an Alberta ULC is an eligible entity and may file Form 8832 to elect to be treated as a partnership or disregarded entity (check-the-box). For Canadian tax purposes, no domestic check-the-box election exists; the ULC is taxable as a corporation. Hybrid mismatch arrangements may be mitigated by section 18.4 and section 18.5 of the Income Tax Act (addressing foreign entity classification mismatches) and by the OECD Multilateral Instrument provisions implemented in the Canada-U.S. Tax Treaty. The CRA treats an Alberta ULC as a Canadian resident corporation; it cannot elect to be transparent for Canadian income tax. For GST/HST purposes, the ULC is a 'person' and a registrant if it makes taxable supplies in Canada; no special fiscal transparency election exists for GST/HST. An Alberta ULC can elect under section 216 of the Income Tax Act (for non-resident owners) only to compute tax on Canadian-source rental income, which is irrelevant to the audio licensing business. For U.S. owners, a ULC can elect to be a disregarded entity for U.S. tax, but Canadian tax remains at the entity level. Alberta does not have a separate check-the-box regime. The entity must file T2 and pay federal and Alberta corporate tax at combined rates unless relief is available under the Canada-U.S. Tax Treaty, which generally does not eliminate Canadian tax on a Canadian-resident ULC's active business income.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax (GST/HST); Alberta applies 5% federal GST only (no provincial sales tax, no HST). Also potentially applies: Québec QST for Québec customers if sufficient nexus, provincial sales tax for other provinces only if the ULC has physical presence or sales exceeding registration thresholds in those provinces (e.g., Manitoba RST, Saskatchewan PST, British Columbia PST). For digital goods and services supplied to Canadian consumers, the regime relevant is GST/HST and the simplified non-resident GST/HST registration framework.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 (the 'small supplier' threshold) in global taxable supplies other than financial services in the preceding four calendar quarters; once exceeded, the ULC must register for GST/HST. A non-resident that is a 'non-registrant' may also be deemed to be carrying on business in Canada and required to register if it solicits orders in Canada or has a Canadian agent. For digital supplies of audio licensing subscriptions to Canadian recipients, a non-resident supplier may be required to register under the mandatory 'registration of non-resident persons carrying on business in Canada' rule if it makes taxable supplies in Canada; however, the special 'specified supplies' regime for non-resident digital service suppliers uses a separate threshold: for supplies of 'specified digital services' (including music downloads and streaming) made to Canadian recipients, a non-resident supplier must register if it is not a small supplier (CAD 30,000) or if it sells more than CAD 30,000 in a calendar quarter to Canadian recipients and does not meet the small supplier exception. New GST/HST rules effective July 1, 2021: non-resident vendors of digital goods and services are required to register, collect, and remit GST/HST on supplies to Canadian consumers unless their worldwide taxable supplies do not exceed CAD 30,000 in any rolling four-quarter period. Since the audio licensing marketplace targets Canadian customers via Stripe/PayPal, the ULC should assume the threshold is CAD 30,000. There is no separate Alberta provincial registration threshold for GST because Alberta has no provincial sales tax; but if the ULC is a 'large business' (generally over CAD 10 million in taxable supplies), it must file GST/HST electronically monthly and may be subject to a penalty for not registering. For zero-rated exports, there is no threshold exception.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not currently impose a mandatory electronic invoicing (e-invoicing) or real-time fiscal clearance regime akin to Latin American models. The CRA accepts electronic invoices if they are legible and contain prescribed information: supplier name, recipient name, GST/HST registration number, invoice date, description, amount, and tax charged. The CRA does not require pre-clearance or digital stamping. Since May 2022, the CRA has published the 'Electronic Payment Standard' and is progressively implementing a 'Digital Compliance' framework using data analytics; business must retain source books and records in an electronically readable format. GST/HST registrants with annual taxable supplies exceeding CAD 5 million must file GST/HST returns electronically; all registrants must use electronic filing if the CRA directs. The CRA mandates a specific GST/HST NETFILE XML format for the GST/HST return itself, but there is no government-validated e-invoicing clearance. However, for any imports into Canada, the CBSA requires electronic customs declarations via the Canadian Single Window and a B3 form or CADEX; commercial goods must be reported through the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management (CARM) portal. For digital services, no fiscal clearance stamp is required. The ULC should implement secure electronic invoicing that complies with Canada's books and records retention rules (Income Tax Act section 230; Excise Tax Act section 286) and must be prepared to produce invoices in English or French. There is no requirement to obtain a CRA-issued 'authorization code' for each invoice. The ULC should use its BN/RT account on invoices.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating applies to exports of tangible personal property under section 1, Part V, Schedule VI to the Excise Tax Act (ETA) when the supplier exports the property by commercial or private carrier and maintains evidence of export. For services and intangible personal property (including licences of copyrighted music or royalty-free stock music), zero-rating applies under section 9 or section 13 of Part V, Schedule VI when the supply is made to a non-resident person who is not registered under the GST/HST and the supply is not acquired for consumption, use, or supply in Canada: specifically, a supply of an intangible right, such as a copyright licence, made to a non-resident is zero-rated if the supply is made to a non-resident who is not a GST/HST registrant, provided the recipient is not acquiring the licence for use in Canada. Royalty-free stock music licensing to foreign end customers is generally zero-rated as a supply of an intangible personal property or a service performed for a non-resident that is not consumed in Canada. Zero-rating eligibility requires the supplier to obtain sufficient evidence that the recipient is a non-resident at the time the tax becomes payable; commonly a written statement from the recipient, commercial contract, IP address, billing address, payment gateway data showing foreign bank/credit card, and the customer's export of any physical delivery. For digital downloads delivered online, no customs export declaration is required, but evidence of delivery to a foreign IP address and non-resident payment method should be retained. For digital supplies of 'specified digital services' to non-residents, zero-rating also applies under subsection 25.1(2) of Part V of Schedule VI if the non-resident recipient is not registered and the supply is not in connection with the recipient's Canadian business. The ULC should obtain a non-resident declaration from each foreign customer through its online checkout flow. Exports of goods are eligible for zero-rating only if shipped from Canada; electronic delivery is treated as an intangible supply and zero-rated.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (B13A / Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) Export Declaration) — required only if the tangible property is physically exported from Canada; not applicable to digital audio downloads, but should be prepared if royalty-free music is delivered on physical media (e.g., USB drives or CDs).

Commercial Invoice — showing supplier name, recipient name and address, description of the licensed music, quantity/consideration, and statement that the supply is zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part V (if applicable).
Bill of Lading or Carrier Receipt (air waybill, courier manifest, or postal receipt) — for physical export shipments, as proof that the goods left Canada.

Non-Resident Declaration (Form GST/HST composite evidence: certificate of residence, foreign address, foreign IP address, foreign payment method/PayPal/Stripe account country, email domain, or signed declaration by the recipient stating the recipient is a non-resident and will not use the supply in Canada).

Inward Remittance Certificate (IRC) or Payment Gateway Transaction Record — evidencing foreign currency conversion and receipt of proceeds from a foreign source (Stripe/PayPal payout documentation, bank statements showing inbound wire from foreign entity).
GST/HST Return (GST/HST NETFILE) and Books and Records Retention Log — substantiating the zero-rated revenue inclusion, if the ULC is a registrant.
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Under the Excise Tax Act, a false or fraudulent claim for zero-rating may result in: (i) reassessment of GST/HST at 5% on the full invoice value, with interest computed under section 280 (daily compounded interest at the prescribed rate); (ii) a penalty of 25% of the amount of tax sought to be evaded under subsection 280(1) for gross negligence; (iii) additional penalties of up to $25,000 or fines up to 200% of the evaded tax under the Tax Court of Canada procedures; (iv) suspension or cancellation of a GST/HST registration; (v) criminal prosecution under section 327(1) of the Excise Tax Act for evading payment or obtaining a refund to which the person is not entitled, punishable by imprisonment of up to 5 years. The CRA may also apply the general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) under section 245 of the Income Tax Act to deny treaty benefits or revoke zero-rating if the transactions are designed to obtain a tax benefit. For exports of tangible property, failure to meet the documentary proof requirements within the prescribed retention period (6 years) results in the supply being recharacterized as taxable in Canada and the registrant is liable for unremitted GST/HST. The 'inward remittance' documentation must be retained for six years from the end of the year, and the CRA may perform a GST/HST audit and conduct a 'validation review' that verifies that the payment was actually received from a non-resident; if the payment is received through a Canadian payment processor or intermediary, the CRA may assert the supply was made in Canada unless the ULC demonstrates the commercial reality is a supply to a non-resident. Penalties can also include an 'unregistered large corporation penalty' of $2,000 per failure to file, plus the usual instalment penalties. Under the Customs Act, any false export declaration in a B13A filing may carry penalties of up to $15,000 for a corporation and forfeiture of goods. Given the low-risk nature of the licensing model, the ULC must implement a robust export substantiation process, recording the customer's non-resident status at each sale and preserving the foreign IP address and payment origin evidence for at least six years.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) in conjunction with the Canadian Department of Finance, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI), and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for cross-border financial intelligence; foreign exchange and capital account administration is principally handled by the Exchange Fund Account managed by the Bank of Canada and the cross-border data reporting framework under the Customs Act and the Currency Declaration Regulations.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: Canada maintains a fully liberalized capital account with no general exchange controls, no restriction on current or capital account transactions, and a freely floating Canadian dollar (CAD). Profits, royalties, service fees, dividends, and capital repatriation from an Alberta-Based Unlimited Liability Corporation (ULC) can be remitted without central bank authorisation. The only mandatory hurdles are PCMLTFA record keeping, large cash transaction reporting (LCTR), and electronic funds transfer reporting (EFTR) for entries/remittances exceeding CAD 10,000 in a single transaction or consecutive transactions intended to evade thresholds. The CAD is fully convertible; there is no differentiated capital vs current account treatment.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no statutory export proceeds surrender requirement and no mandatory conversion ratio to CAD. Exporters and cross-border licensors may retain all foreign currency proceeds in foreign-denominated accounts maintained in Canada or abroad. The only obligations relate to transfer pricing contemporaneous documentation under the Income Tax Act, Section 247, and submission of Canadian Balance of Payments transaction reports through Statistics Canada for inbound/outbound payments exceeding CAD 1,000,000 annually, where applicable. There is no specific timeline for converting export receipts; banks may establish internal policy requiring declaration of foreign currency receipts for reporting under the Foreign Exchange Accounting Framework (managed by OSFI).

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility Rating: HIGH for ancillary collection rails on royalty-free stock music subscriptions and Soundscape licensing fees; LOW for primary treasury account holding. Canadian-regulated Financial Technology Entities (e.g., Wise, Payoneer, Stripe) and provincial Money Services Businesses may provide payment facilitation, but they are not Canadian Schedule I banks and cannot serve as the primary bank account for a ULC requiring statutory capital escrow, dividend distributions, or CRA direct debit relationships. Offshore EMIs without registration under the Retail Payment Activities Act or while required licenses are pending, are not viable as principal corporate bank accounts. They may be used as receiving-node only, with full sweep to a domestic Tier-1 account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Federal anti-money-laundering rules do not mandate a mandatory physical appearance for corporate KYC interviews; FINTRAC guidance permits remote ID verification using a recognized Dealer in Financial Services. However, most Canadian Schedule I banks, when onboarding a foreign-director Alberta ULC with cross-border capital flows, will require a video interview with specific ID scanning, remote verification of registered office and directorships, and in certain cases an in-person visit to a Canadian branch or notarial certification by a Canadian consulate. For fully remote opening, a corporate search report from Alberta Corporate Registry, certified apostilled articles, and a banker’s reference from the ULC’s existing principal bank must be submitted. Feasibility of purely remote onboarding: MEDIUM for an Alberta ULC; enhanced due diligence is acceptable.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Beneficial Owner or Ultimate Beneficiary (UBO) resident in a high-risk or non- FATF-compliant jurisdiction, causing enhanced risk scoring.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified passport and residence permit of the UBO; source-of-funds bank statements (last 6 months); tax residency certificate from the UBO's jurisdiction; corporate organisational chart with percentage ownership tracked to natural persons; signed AML attestation; and notarised Power of Attorney identifying the Canadian signatory.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: ULC pass-through classification creating ambiguous beneficial ownership structure and failure to identify all founding members and equity subscribers.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Shareholder register, fully updated; escrow agreement for capital subscription; subscription letters; legal opinion from a Canadian counsel confirming the ULC's unlimited liability and pass-through status; registry extract from Alberta Corporate Registry; consent of each member to KYC disclosure.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large inbound payments from music subscription platforms and commission payments to global licensing partners, triggering a pattern of frequent cross-border EFTs requiring FINTRAC reporting.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Commercial licensing contracts for royalty-free stock music; platform payout reports from Stripe/PayPal; proof of contractual fee schedule; complete sales ledger; master service agreements with music distributors; and tax invoice records demonstrating beneficial ownership of the intellectual property.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Capital Escrow Account receipt of a high-value wire from a foreign parent or founding shareholder with non-banking intermediary funding.
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Authorised share subscription agreement; bank-to-bank wire confirmation; Certified source-of-funding declaration; signed board resolution approving the capital injection; copy of the intercompany agreement; and abroad-issued due diligence questionnaire answered and witnessed.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Compliant routing uses SWIFT MT103 or SWIFT MT202 for the transfer to an Alberta-based Tier-1 bank account. The payment must be clearly labelled with purpose code ‘CA200 – Equity Injection’ or use ISO 20022 purpose code INVE/IVGT (Investment). FINTRAC requires an EFT report for a single transfer of CAD 10,000 or more. The following documentation must accompany the wire instruction: certified copy of the ULC articles, board resolution approving the capital contribution, share subscription agreement, source-of-funds declaration by the remitting member, and a covered funds or CIP attestation from the remitting bank. No central bank permission is required, but the receiving bank will require a Bank of Canada cheque or electronic clearance via Lynx for same-day CAD settlement; if the capital is in USD, the Canadian bank will convert to CAD using the floating exchange rate at delivery, unless a hedging forward is pre-arranged.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: For royalty-free stock music licensing royalty payouts to foreign copyright owners, use SWIFT MT103 with purpose code ‘Royalties’ (Category S–General Services) and populate Field 70 to include the licensing contract number. For high-value trade settlements, Canadian banks issue irrevocable documentary credits (Commercial LC) via SWIFT MT700; the beneficiary’s bank presents complying documents via MT760/MT707 as appropriate. For recurring subscription fees paid to foreign distribution platforms, use same-day CAD clearing via Lynx and cross-border USD via international ACH through a clearing house linking SWIFT; for disbursements above CAD 5 million, consider direct correspondent bank transfers via a Canadian Clearing Practice (CCP) using MT101 and central settlement. All outbound payments must be subject to FINTRAC EFT reporting over CAD 10,000, and sanction/sanctions-list screening is required.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable CAD/USD forward contracts with a Canadian Schedule I bank (non-speculative, bespoke or exchange-traded FX forwards)
Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for non-fully-convertible currencies settled in CAD, requiring ISDA with a Canadian counterparty
Cross-currency interest rate swaps (CCIRS) for managing long-term net royalty and subscription income cash flows
Rolling spot-dated FX swaps (overnight rollovers) to manage temporary payment mismatches
Outright foreign currency options (put/call) on permissible currencies, provided derivatives use is cash-flow hedging and documented under IFRS 9 hedge accounting
Warrant and strike-forward hybrid instruments executed through the dealer’s treasury desk, subject to internal board approval and prudent risk limits

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 days after the corporation's registration anniversary date each year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing incurs CAD 50 penalty; continued non-filing beyond two consecutive years triggers administrative dissolution or strike-off.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: No later than 6 months after the fiscal year-end (Alberta ULC is treated as a corporation for domestic tax purposes)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty is 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per month (up to 12 months); repeated failure incurs additional 10% penalty; compound interest applies to unpaid amounts.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No mandatory audit applies solely for gross revenue or assets to a private (non-distributing) Alberta ULC; audit may be waived by unanimous shareholder consent each financial year. A court, regulator, or shareholder application can nonetheless compel an audit.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian GAAP: either IFRS or Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises (ASPE); ASPE is the default for a private ULC not listed on a stock exchange.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta Corporate Registry does not receive a public annual UBO filing. The ULC must, however, maintain a securities register at its registered office and record all share transfers promptly; on an annual basis the corporate secretary should prepare a resolution confirming the shareholder register and any transfers of significant interest (≥25%) for the minutes.

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% combined (federal 15% + Alberta 8%). For Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) claiming the Small Business Deduction, the combined effective rate on active business income up to C$500,000 is 17% (federal 9% + Alberta 8%).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: Small Business Deduction (SBD) reducing federal tax from 15% to 9% on CCPC active business income up to C$500,000; accelerated capital cost allowance (CCA) for computing and eligible capital equipment; scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) investment tax credits for qualifying digital audio software R&D. No statutory corporate income tax holiday applies in Alberta for audio licensing marketplaces.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed electronically via CRA Corporation Internet Filing (EFILE/XML), third-party tax software, or through a registered tax preparer portal.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (T2 return filed once per taxation year); quarterly corporate instalment payments are required in prescribed circumstances.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 must be filed within 6 months after the end of the corporation's taxation year. For a December 31 year-end, the deadline is June 30 of the following calendar year. Instalment payments are due on the 15th day of the 2nd month after the year-end and the 15th day of the 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th months of the taxation year for qualifying corporations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Corporation identification: legal name, CRA Business Number, date of incorporation, country of incorporation (Canada/Alberta), and tax year-end.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Provide the Alberta registered office address and confirm the corporation is resident in Canada for treaty purposes. Non-resident ULC shareholders do not file the T2 on behalf of the corporation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Taxable income computation: worldwide income including stock-music subscription revenue, royalty/licensing fees, and ancillary sales, less allowable expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Revenue must be recognized per Canadian GAAP. A ULC controlled by non-residents remains taxable on worldwide income unless a tax treaty tie-breaker applies.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net income before tax adjustments as computed under section 3 of the Income Tax Act.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Prepare financial statements on Canadian GAAP. Transfer pricing adjustments must be made before filing if non-arm's-length cross-border transactions exceed thresholds.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Small Business Deduction claim: 9% federal deduction on the lesser of active business income and C$500,000 business limit.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the ULC is controlled by one or more non-resident persons, it is not a CCPC and cannot claim the SBD. Confirm shareholding composition prior to claiming.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provincial corporate tax allocation and Alberta taxable income computation at 8%.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Allocate income to Alberta based on the location of permanent establishments and gross revenue attribution. Non-resident-controlled ULCs with foreign PE should file the Alberta AT1 corporate tax return separately if required.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Refundable dividend tax on hand balances and dividend refund calculations.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Any dividend paid to a non-resident parent triggers Part XIII withholding at the applicable treaty rate; RDTOH does not eliminate the Part XIII obligation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Capital cost allowance on intangible assets (computer software, audiovisual production, licensing platforms) and equipment.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Ensure acquired intangible assets from non-residents are recorded at fair market value and supported by a transfer pricing analysis.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty under s.162(1): 5% of balance owing plus 1% per complete month up to 12 months, minimum C$100. Gross negligence penalty under s.163(2): 50% of understated tax. Daily compound interest under s.161 at CRA prescribed rates applies to unpaid amounts. Penalties for late T106/T1134/T1135 information returns apply separately, up to C$2,500 and C$8,000 per return respectively.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% Part XIII withholding tax on dividends paid by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident shareholder. Reduced treaty rates apply generally: 5% for U.S. corporate shareholders holding at least 10% voting shares under Article 10, 15% for portfolio shareholders; 5%/15% under most other Canadian DTAs.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the ULC must obtain a properly completed NR301 (for U.S. residents) or NR302 (for other treaty countries) declaration from the non-resident beneficial owner, together with a valid Certificate of Residence (e.g., IRS Form 6166 for U.S. residents). The forms must be in CRA's possession before or at the time of filing the NR4 withholding return. The treaty's Limitation on Benefits clause must be satisfied; otherwise the statutory 25% rate applies and excess withholding may be refunded via an NR7-R application.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory withholding: 25% on royalties, including copyright, sound recording, digital audio licensing and software royalties; 25% on interest, subject to specific exemptions. Under the Canada-U.S. treaty: most copyright royalties are exempt from Canadian withholding (0%) under Article 12; interest is generally exempt (0%) under Article 11 for U.S. residents in arm's-length transactions. Under other Canadian DTAs, royalty withholding is typically 0% or 10% and interest is typically 0% or 10%, depending on the beneficial ownership and treaty particulars.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: C$1,000,000. A Canadian corporation must file Form T106 and prepare contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation when its reportable transactions with any non-resident related party exceed C$1,000,000 in the taxation year. CRA generally follows OECD transfer pricing documentation standards, including Master File and Local File expectations.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Applicable through Canadian GAAR (s.245 of the Income Tax Act) and the OECD-aligned transfer pricing rules. Transactions must have real economic substance, purposeful business rationale, and arm's-length economic returns. Alberta does not operate offshore Economic Substance Regulations, but hybrid entity structures (ULC check-the-box) require substantive commercial activity, proper staffing, Canadian decision-making, and actual risk assumption to withstand CRA anti-avoidance review and treaty LOB scrutiny.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Wilfully underreporting stock-music licensing revenue, fabricating expenses, using hidden offshore bank accounts, failing to file T2/NR4/T106 returns, or knowingly making false statements to the CRA.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Fine under s.239 of the Income Tax Act of up to 200% of the tax evaded plus imprisonment up to 5 years. Civil penalty under s.163(2) of 50% of understated tax. Accrued interest and revocation of eligibility for voluntary disclosure.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly participate in or authorize evasion are liable to criminal prosecution, personal fines and imprisonment. Personal remittance liability under s.227.1 applies for unremitted withholdings. Civil fraudulent conveyance judgments may pierce the corporate veil. Travel bans or departure orders may be issued under s.226 of the ITA for unpaid assessed tax.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Charging non-arm's-length royalty fees to a foreign parent for nominal IP, allocating excessive profit to a low-tax jurisdiction through intercompany licensing, or failing to maintain contemporaneous documentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: CRA reassessment under s.247 to arm's-length prices; 10% transfer pricing penalty on the adjustment amount if documentation is inadequate; interest on deficiencies; potential criminal prosecution for grossly negligent misrepresentation.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who approve or sign false transfer pricing documentation face personal civil liability; in insolvency scenarios the CRA may seek director assessments for unremitted amounts; criminal liability for aiding in tax evasion.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the ULC as a hybrid entity to create double deductions or payments that are deductible in one jurisdiction for U.S. purposes but not taxed in Canada, such as through an ill-conceived check-the-box election without economic substance.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Anti-hybrid rules under s.18.4/18.5 disallow deductions; GAAR under s.245 denies the tax benefit; treaty refusal under LOB clauses; Part XIII assessments on deemed dividends; 50% gross negligence penalty; potential FAPI inclusion for shareholders.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who structure sham hybrid transactions with knowledge face personal assessments and criminal exposure; courts may disregard the ULC's separate legal identity if it is a facade; travel bans and asset freezing orders are available in serious cases.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Money Laundering / Unlicensed Cross-Border Payment Processing
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating a payment marketplace through Stripe/PayPal without FINTRAC registration where the business constitutes a money services business; deliberately obscuring beneficiary ownership or moving revenue through shell entities/mixed crypto channels to evade corporate tax obligations.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Administrative monetary penalties up to C$500,000 per violation; criminal penalties under the Criminal Code (up to 10 years imprisonment) for laundering proceeds; forfeiture orders; prohibition from serving as corporate director.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who direct or approve money laundering are criminally liable as principals; personal fines and imprisonment; travel bans imposed as bail conditions or part of restraining orders; assets subject to restraint and forfeiture.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Unreported Foreign Affiliate / Foreign Reporting Failures
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Holding a non-Canadian parent, financing subsidiary, or IP holding company without filing Form T1134 (Foreign Affiliate Information Return) or Form T1135 (Foreign Income Verification Statement), or failing to report Canada-source subscription revenue routed through a foreign platform entity.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: T1135: C$25/day up to C$2,500; for knowing failure C$500 to C$12,000. T1134: C$100/day up to C$8,000. Additional penalties for failure to respond to demand up to C$24,000. Reassessment plus interest.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly fail to file may be personally assessed for penalties; if foreign reporting was used to conceal taxable income, directors face criminal tax evasion liability and personal fines; CRA departure orders may apply for ongoing delinquent accounts.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating the ULC as a pure pass-through shell: no real employees, no Canadian office, no substantive contracts, all decision-making and stock-music licensing activities performed from outside Canada, with the sole purpose of using the ULC as a conduit to defer or avoid tax.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: GAAR reassessment under s.245; denial of treaty benefits; corporate veil-piercing under provincial and federal corporate law; penalties for failure to maintain corporate registration (annual return defaults); potential revocation of incorporation status and director disqualification.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Under Alberta and British Columbia ULC statutes, shareholders have unlimited liability; directors may be personally liable for corporate debts where the ULC was treated as an agent or sham. Directors can be assessed without benefit of corporate shield for unpaid taxes, GST/HST, and employee source deductions; travel bans under s.226 for leaving Canada while debts to the CRA exceed C$10,000.
